endorsements.quote: Intended use and scope : specific indications (for example, prioritising ICU consults, drafting progress notes, supporting family communication) with narrow definitions; explicit exclusions (no autonomous treatment decisions, no independent allocation of scarce life-support resources, no override of clinical judgment); and the precise population and setting (adult versus paediatric units, mixed versus specialised ICUs, elective versus emergency admissions).

Position in the decision-making hierarchy : whether outputs are advisory, partially binding, or automated; which clinicians may act on them and under what supervision; and how disagreements between model recommendations and clinical judgment are resolved and documented.

Each deployed model should have documentation analogous to a device label, including a concise statement of purpose and limits, a summary of training data, key validation metrics, and known limitations or biases.

Because ICUs are dynamic environments, ongoing performance monitoring is essential: regular assessment of discrimination and calibration on recent cases, visibility of drift indicators to governance bodies and, where possible, frontline staff, and predefined thresholds for pausing or withdrawing a model when performance or safety concerns arise.

Patient-facing transparency also matters once tools move from retrospective research to real-time care: institutions should decide how to inform patients or surrogates about AI-assisted tools and how their data may be used for model improvement, in line with legal and ethical standards.

All users should acquire foundational AI literacy, including basic concepts of pre-training and fine-tuning, common failure modes such as hallucinations, data drift and bias, and the distinction between predictive correlations and causal reasoning.

Role-specific competencies are also needed: bedside nurses should learn to recognise when LLM-generated triage suggestions conflict with direct observation and how to escalate; residents and fellows should practise integrating outputs into care plans and handovers; consultants and leaders should be equipped to interpret dashboards, participate in governance, and mentor junior staff.
ensuring governance committees include clinicians, nurses, data scientists, ethicists and, where feasible, patient representatives
this means linking models to specific workflow problems (such as triage bottlenecks or documentation burden)
designing pilots that assess not only technical performance but also clinician trust, workflow fit, and unintended consequences.
which performance metrics (for example, area under the curve, F1-scores, calibration, and subgroup analyses) are routinely communicated to staff [ 2 ].

unlisted_practices: State what a summarisation preprocessing step prioritises or discards and how full records can be accessed in any LLM deployment using summarisation.
Train users to ask for transparency about training data, validation, limitations, and domain of use, and to interpret calibration and subgroup performance.
Use scenario-based training with retrospective cases so clinicians practise interpreting and challenging LLM suggestions and recognising warning signs.

screen.reason: This is an editorial providing recommendations and a practice-oriented framework for the governance, instructions for use, and safe deployment of LLMs in critical and perioperative care.
